entry.title: My monitor was cutting my download speed by 75%
entry.content:
My Monitor Was Cutting My Download Speed by 75%

Somehow I am one of those few very lucky people to have the opportunity of owning a 2.5 gig symmetrical line for my internet. But one day, when I wanted to brag to my equally nerdy friends, shock and horror: 600 Mbps down? Luckily my upload speed was still 2.4 Gbps, so I didn’t lose all my bragging rights, but that’s weird, right? If anything, you’d expect the opposite!

My ISP is pretty cool. It’s run by this one guy (Hey Keith!), and I know I can always message them and they respond promptly, as they did this time. We tried to run through a few debugging steps, they checked on their end, and everything was normal. I tried my work laptop too, same speed.

I didn’t have time for debugging, because I needed to travel 2000 km to the other side of the continent for a family emergency.

But as soon as I got back, I got curious again. What could it be? In retrospect, I now know when it started: when I moved all my connections onto my Studio Display XDR. I wanted to have a one-cable setup, and the monitor offered me that. I’ve had it for half a year now, and I don’t think I’ve ever run a speed test through it. 600 Mbps was more than fast enough for me to never realise I wasn’t getting three quarters of the speed I was paying for 🤦

The setup# MacBook Pro M3 Pro 2026 Studio Display XDR, with everything plugged into it so switching laptops is one cable UGREEN USB-C to 2.5G Ethernet adapter, plugged into the display UniFi Dream Router 7, the same one from my WiFi 7 debugging post What I thought was interesting#

Pings to other wired computers during a download would fail 10% of the time over Ethernet through the adapter plugged into my screen, and 0% of the time over Wi-Fi. What made it stranger was that there were no dropped frame errors in macOS’s logs at all. This was the big hint for me: the adapter was dropping them before the computer could know.

I then plugged the adapter straight into my Mac instead of the monitor, and ran an iperf3 server on my UDR 7: 2.3 Gbps. So the cable, the router and the adapter are all fine? What about fast.com? Perfect speeds there too! 2.2 down and 2.3 up when connected straight in. As soon as I connected it to the display, it was back to 600 down again.

So it’s the display, right? Well, I would find out: sort of yes, sort of no, which is why I wanted to write this blog post. I couldn’t find anything online explaining the exact cause, and it’s quite a cool reason.

The driver and flow control#

The adapter uses a Realtek RTL8156B, which on macOS binds to Apple’s generic USB networking driver. But Realtek ship their own driver on their website, so I thought I’d give that a go! I installed it and, to my surprise, it almost doubled the download speed to 1.1 Gbps, but that was still nowhere close to 2.5. First hint that it couldn’t just be the monitor’s fault.

Then I tried flow control. I had never truly looked into this before, and I think it’s quite neat to know about if you were also ignorant of it like me. Basically, when a device receives Ethernet frames it can’t keep up with, it just drops them. With flow control (it’s something your router or switch has to support), it can send the sender a “pause” frame, and the sender then buffers the data on its side, instead of the receiver (the adapter in this case) on its side. I turned it on in my UniFi console and guess what, download jumped to around 2 Gbps, with upload still at full speed! Yay! Well, not so fast…

I don’t like it always being on, because it can add latency to other systems like my gaming PC. Can you work around it? For sure, you can disable it on those computers, but it’s janky, and it’s another thing I need to remember when my Sauerbraten game starts lagging. I need fewer things to remember, considering I am 30 in a couple of months. My memory is not what it used to be.

But the upload was always fine#

Yeah, isn’t that weird? First of all, it looks like the port can indeed do 2.5 in both directions. I already knew that, because I get much more than that from my external SSD through the monitor’s Thunderbolt port. So the issue is not the monitor again? But it has to be!

Well, I had another idea. How about I connect to my Linux box, which is also on 2.5, and send perfectly smooth UDP traffic at a fixed rate with flow control off? Then I can check the chip’s own counter of dropped frames:

Sent Lost behind the display Frames/s reaching the Mac behind the display Lost direct on the Mac 1.46 Gbps 0% 123,800 0% 1.75 Gbps 0.05% 148,600 0% 1.94 Gbps 0.1% 165,000 0% 2.03 Gbps 2.7% 168,000 0% 2.12 Gbps 7.2% 168,000 0% 2.20 Gbps 10.5% 168,000 0.001% 2.28 Gbps 13.5% 168,000 0.02%

So basically no drops whatsoever when connected straight to my Mac, but loads of drops after about 168k frames per second (roughly 2 Gbps). Remember that number. That number comes from the adapter’s own counters: however much I sent, the number of frames it managed to hand over to the Mac each second flattened out at about 168,000, and everything above that was dropped.

Why did this not happen on my SSD? What was the only difference I could find? Bursts!

When the Mac reads data from a USB 3 device, the device sends some packets, then has to wait for the Mac to say “lgtm, send more!”. The SSD enclosure sends 16 packets before needing a go-ahead message back. The RTL8156B in my Ethernet adapter sends 4.

Here is a diagram of my best understanding of why this is an issue. I made this diagram 100 times, and I think I can probably improve it more, but if it helps you understand the issue, I have done my job.

As you can see, the speed of packets coming into the adapter is 2.5 Gbps. That’s what the router pushes in. The speed going out is around 2 Gbps. The reason is that if you add up the average time it takes to get the go-ahead through my monitor’s hub, which is around 7.6 µs, to the average time it takes to send 4 KB, around 8.2 µs, you can find what the maximum speed is.

Well, if the speed of the drain from my adapter to my Mac is half a gig slower than the speed of the input, then you can imagine the buffer getting filled more and more until it overflows. Those are dropped packets, which result in a hard backoff when the router resends them, so you drop loads in speed. And that’s the reason for all of this.

OK, well, what now?#

I have a cupboard full of USB-C Ethernet adapters. Don’t ask.

The problem is they’re all 1 gig adapters, so any of the tests I made would not tell me anything, because the issues don’t start at 1 gig. They start at around 2… If I run my 2.5 gig adapter at 1 gig speeds, I get 1 gig downloads with the official driver. If I run it at 1.5, I get 1.5. If I run it at 2, well, I get 1…

So I thought I would do what any human would do, and I spent more money on a new adapter. Another UGREEN, but this time it’s one that promises 5 Gbps and uses the RTL8157 chip instead: UGREEN 5G USB-C Ethernet adapter. My reasoning was that if this one could get me better speeds, it would help me understand how. And that it did!

With this adapter, I dropped 0 frames:

Sent Frames/s reaching the Mac Dropped by the adapter 1.5 Gbps 124k 0 1.9 Gbps 157k 0 2.1 Gbps 173k 0 2.3 Gbps 187k 0 2.4 Gbps 194k 0

Why? Well, looking through what each adapter tells me about itself:

$ python3 -c "import usb.core; e = usb.core.find(idVendor=0x0bda)[0][(0,0)][0]; print('packet size', e.wMaxPacketSize, 'bMaxBurst', e.extra_descriptors[2])" # old adapter (RTL8156B) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 3 # new adapter (RTL8157) packet size 1024 bMaxBurst 7 # bMaxBurst counts the packets after the first one, so 3 means 4 packets and 7 means 8

I can see that instead of sending 4 1 KB packets per burst, it would send 8! And the speed of the link was also 2x faster, so those 8 KB would go 2x faster to the Mac. That means the time spent was 8 times lower to send the same data, and while the wait for the go-ahead was identical, the theoretical speed from the adapter to the Mac, including the wait for the go-ahead, was a maximum of 4.5 Gbps. That’s much bigger than the 2.5 coming into the adapter, so the buffer would never fill up, packets would never drop and everything was great, even if the “go-ahead” response was still much slower than when connected directly to the Mac.

Final thoughts#

I think the big takeaway from this is that all the things you think are quite easy to understand, such as transfer speeds, have so many cool intricacies that it’s worth diving deep every so often. Who would’ve thought that the speed of the link between the adapter and the Mac was defined not only by the link speed itself in Gbps, but also by the time it took your Mac to reply, by the amount of packets, by the speed of those packets, by the number of packets in a burst, and by the size of those packets?

See you next time, when I will spend just as much time on another trivial thing that we can all learn from!

Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis
entry.content:
Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis Lean verification of the Riemann Hypothesis

Joint statement by the Lean and Mathlib communities, endorsed by the Lean FRO and the Mathlib Initiative.

On November 20, 2026, Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library comprising 17 million lines of code.

We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement.

Our rationale is outlined below.

The codebase depends directly only on Mathlib. Over the past day, the Lean and Mathlib communities have rallied to verify the proof's correctness. We hereby certify that both the statement and the proof of the Riemann Hypothesis are correct. The four criteria in https://xenaproject.wordpress.com/2026/11/12/and-the-proof-is-checked-in-lean/ are all satisfied.

The statement of the Riemann Hypothesis is correct. This statement is part of Mathlib: RiemannHypothesis and has been carefully vetted by experts in Lean and number theory. Alpöge’s library compiles correctly. By now, dozens of people have reported correct compilation of the codebase, reproducing the same raw proof export file. The library compiles without errors or build failures. The code proves the correct statement. Crucially, the community has added a file that isolates the statement of the Riemann Hypothesis and imports only Mathlib. That statement was compared against the theorem proved by Alpöge using two independent tools (comparator and con-leche –compare), both confirming that the theorem proved in Alpöge’s library is exactly Mathlib’s statement of the Riemann Hypothesis. The Lean proof is valid. The exported raw proof has been checked by several proof checkers, including Lean’s official kernel, the con-leche and con-ron checkers, and several independent checkers contributed by third parties and implemented in different programming languages. The checkers con-leche and con-ron come with a formal proof, relative to set theory, that they cannot accept a false proof, thus addressing concerns that Lean’s logic itself might have flaws that the proof could exploit. An extensive overview is available at https://math.mit.edu/~drew/grh/. These checks ran on an inert export of the proof, out of reach of hypothetical malicious code in the Lean proof sources.

Thanks are owed to everyone in the community who provided resources for the verification.

We look forward to all the activity in the mathematical community that will help explain the new ideas in this proof.

entry.title: Show HN: Zero C# – C# without a runtime or GC
entry.content:
C# with nothing underneath

A fork of bflat compiles C# straight to a small native program: no .NET runtime, no garbage collector, nothing to install where it runs.

You keep C#'s syntax, type checking and generics. Memory comes from arenas you free all at once, and a small library gives you strings, collections, input and output on those terms. The same source runs on Linux, macOS and Windows, on WebAssembly, and on DOS on a 386.

// Read into a stack buffer: nothing allocated per answer. Span<char> buffer = stackalloc char[32]; Out.Write($"Q{i}: {a} + {b} = "); int length = In.ReadLine(buffer); // Kept until the end, so it goes into an arena. mistakes.Add(Str.Format(keep, $"{a} + {b} = {a + b}, not {value}")); The language stays, the runtime goes

The compiler still checks everything it checks in .NET. What's missing is what a runtime would do while your program runs.

You keep C# 15Unions, extension members and the new memory safety rules. Real genericsA specialized copy for each type, and static abstract members. Interfaces and virtual methodsDefault interface methods, casts, is and as. Records, tuples, anonymous typesValue equality, with, and the generated ToString. Lambdas and queriesWhere, Select and GroupBy, from a small library instead of LINQ. ThreadsParallel.For runs a loop on every core. You do without Garbage collectorArenas free their memory all at once, when you say. .NET runtimeHello world is 11 KB on Windows and 40 KB on Linux, with nothing to install. Catching exceptionsthrow ends the program. Return errors as unions. Reflection and asyncA type can be compared, but it has no name. One program, five machines

The hello-world sample, unchanged, built for each target. Each build is checked by the same test suite, which requires the same output everywhere.

$ ./build.sh Minimal $ ./run.sh Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/Minimal 39848 bin/Minimal Linux, x64 or arm64

A native program that needs only the C library. On macOS it builds and runs in a container.

$ ./build.sh --mac Minimal $ bin/mac/Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/mac/Minimal 64728 bin/mac/Minimal macOS on Apple Silicon

A native Mac program: bflat compiles it, the Mac's own clang links it. No container to run it.

$ ./build.sh --win Minimal $ ./run.sh --win Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/win/Minimal.exe 10752 bin/win/Minimal.exe Windows x64

A console program on Windows' own C library, built from Linux or macOS. Tested under Wine.

$ ./build.sh --wasm Minimal $ ./run.sh --wasm Minimal Hello from zero-mode! $ wc -c bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm 15833 bin/wasm/Minimal.wasm WebAssembly

A WASI module, through NativeAOT-LLVM. Runs under wasmtime.

C:\>D: D:\>PROGRAM Hello from zero-mode! D:\>DIR PROGRAM.EXE PROGRAM EXE 16,384 D:\> DOS on a 386

The same bitcode compiled for a 386, run by the HX DOS extender. Tested on Bochs's i386 model.

What's different, and what you get

Without a runtime, a few things work differently. Each has a page that explains why and what to do instead.

Memory is yours to free

There is no garbage collector, so new is never freed. Arenas hand out memory and free it all at once, one per lifetime.

Memory without a garbage collector Text without throwaway strings

Out.Line($"...") formats straight into the output buffer, and In.ReadLine reads into a span. Strings that must last go into an arena.

Strings without a garbage collector Collections that live in arenas

List, Dict, and their versions for references and string keys, all handles into an arena.

Choose a collection C# 15, with the safety rules on

Every program compiles under the updated memory safety rules: creating a pointer is safe, reading through one is marked and explained.

The memory safety rules Where to start

If you're new to it, these four pages take you from nothing to an interactive program.

Install

With dotnet on Linux or Windows, or from the repository for every target.

 Your first program

Build it, run it, see how small it is.

 Run it on DOS

The same program under FreeDOS, in an emulator.

 The tutorial

A quiz: output, input, bad input, arenas.

Looking for something specific? The task guides answer one question each, and the reference lists every type in the library.

Verification files for the Lean proof of the Riemann Hypothesis

Announced at alpo.ge/remark.pdf on 20 November 2026.

Andrew Sutherland (MIT), checks run with Claude Code. Page last updated 2026-11-22 04:35 UTC. Results below are as of that time and this page will be updated as the remaining checks finish.

Summary

The published Lean source compiles without errors, the five headline theorems depend only on the three standard axioms, every module has been replayed through the Lean kernel, two independently written kernels, nanoda and con-leche, accept the full exported proof, and lean4lean accepts every compiled module. The --compare modes of con-leche and of its Rust port con-ron, independent implementations of Comparator's statement matching, each confirm all five theorems against the challenge. An independent sandboxed lake build of the archive reproduces the export byte for byte. The lake comparator run and the Lean-kernel replay of the export are still in progress.

(log, log) lean4lean bundled with Lean v4.36.0 not applicable cannot read a v4.33 core library (unknown constant 'Decidable.intro')
What was verified

Five theorems, proved in the submission's Main.lean. Their statements are below exactly as they appear in the challenge file, which imports only Mathlib. All the mathematical notions in them (riemannZeta, DirichletCharacter, DirichletCharacter.LFunction, IsPrimitive) are Mathlib's.

1. The Riemann Hypothesis, using Mathlib's own definition (Mathlib/NumberTheory/LSeries/RiemannZeta.lean): every zero of ζ other than the trivial zeros −2, −4, −6, … has real part 1/2. The condition s ≠ 1 is there because Mathlib assigns ζ a conventional value at its pole.

def RiemannHypothesis : Prop := ∀ (s : ℂ) (_ : riemannZeta s = 0) (_ : ¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * (n + 1)) (_ : s ≠ 1), s.re = 1 / 2 theorem riemannHypothesis : RiemannHypothesis

2. The same statement written out in the submission's own words. Lean accepts the two as equal by definition.

theorem riemannZeta_eq_zero_re : ∀ s : ℂ, riemannZeta s = 0 → (¬∃ n : ℕ, s = -2 * ((n : ℂ) + 1)) → s ≠ 1 → s.re = 1 / 2

3. No zeros to the right of the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function. For every modulus N ≥ 1 and every Dirichlet character χ modulo N, primitive or not, L(χ, s) ≠ 0 whenever Re s > 1/2. The one excluded case is the trivial character at s = 1, where the L-function has its pole.

theorem LFunction_ne_zero_of_half_lt_re : ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ), 1 / 2 < s.re → (χ ≠ 1 ∨ s ≠ 1) → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s ≠ 0

4. Zeros in the critical strip lie on the critical line, for every Dirichlet L-function.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re : ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N) (s : ℂ), 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

5. The same for primitive characters, the form in which the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis for Dirichlet L-functions is usually stated.

theorem LFunction_eq_zero_re_of_isPrimitive : ∀ (N : ℕ) [NeZero N] (χ : DirichletCharacter ℂ N), χ.IsPrimitive → ∀ s : ℂ, 0 < s.re → s.re < 1 → DirichletCharacter.LFunction χ s = 0 → s.re = 1 / 2

Scope. "GRH" here means Dirichlet L-functions: all moduli and all characters. Dedekind zeta functions, Hecke L-functions and automorphic L-functions in general are not among the statements that were checked.

Arithmetic consequences

As a check that does not depend on Mathlib's definition of the zeta function, the proof was combined with kimihiro64/Robin1984 (commit acab1a3), an independent formalization of Robin's and Lagarias's criteria on the same Lean and Mathlib versions. Importing both gives two theorems about the divisor sum, with no hypotheses and no mention of zeta (ArithSolution.lean; statements alone in ArithChallenge.lean, which imports only Mathlib):

theorem robin_inequality : ∀ n : ℕ, 5040 < n → ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) < Real.exp Real.eulerMascheroniConstant * (n : ℝ) * Real.log (Real.log (n : ℝ)) theorem lagarias_inequality : ∀ n : ℕ, 0 < n → ((ArithmeticFunction.sigma 1 n : ℕ) : ℝ) ≤ (harmonic n : ℝ) + Real.exp (harmonic n : ℝ) * Real.log (harmonic n : ℝ) Robin1984 on its own (its three equivalences with RH) Result Detail Robin1984 builds with lake build pass 4,435 jobs, exit 0 con-leche master and --compare accepts 69,293 declarations accepted; all three theorems justified against its own challenge (log) Unmodified Comparator v4.33.0 with the repository's own config pass nanoda accepts, Lean default kernel accepts, "Your solution is okay!"; exit 0 at 03:31:06 UTC (log summary) lake comparator (Lean v4.36.0) from exports pass Lean paranoid kernel, nanoda and Lean default kernel all accept; "Your solution is okay!"; exit 0 at 04:16:52 UTC (log summary)
The two inequalities (RH proof combined with Robin1984) Result Detail robin_inequality and lagarias_inequality compile; #print axioms pass propext, Classical.choice, Quot.sound only (audit) con-leche master on the full combined export accepts 1,472,825 declarations accepted in --verified mode; exit 0 at 02:29:56 UTC (log) con-leche --compare against ArithChallenge accepts both theorems "justified by the solution"; exit 0 at 02:29:06 UTC (log) con-ron --compare (master, 3f22699b) against ArithChallenge accepts both theorems "justified by the solution"; 1,472,825 solution declarations accepted; exit 0 at 23:15:58 UTC on 21 November (log) nanoda on the full combined export accepts exit 0 at 02:56:46 UTC; 33 min 46 s on 64 threads (log) lake comparator (Lean v4.36.0) on the combined export running statement comparison and axiom check passed; its Lean kernel stages are single-threaded on a 62 GB export and are expected to take many hours, as for the main proof

The combined export is 61,752,134,938 bytes, sha256 44651dcc482a6e06e8d626994221aff638e422fded189bf856e0c31176926f0d; its challenge export has sha256 088a57c9e7454fa5279a86a825e551828ac8431694855aadd1f6e6a6eb37bb1d. These statements still rely on Mathlib's definitions of the divisor sum, Euler's constant, harmonic numbers, exp and log, and on the Robin1984 proof, which is why that proof was put through the same checks.

The elaborated statement of the Lagarias inequality

The kernels check elaborated terms, not source text, so what was verified is the term that Lean's elaborator produces from the statement. For the Lagarias inequality that term is short enough to read in full. This is the statement with every coercion, instance and implicit argument shown, as elaborated against Mathlib alone (Lean v4.33.1, Mathlib 0df444a3), with none of the proof loaded:

def lagariasStmt : Prop := ∀ (n : Nat), @LT.lt Nat instLTNat (@OfNat.ofNat Nat (nat_lit 0) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 0))) n → @LE.le Real Real.instLE (@Nat.cast Real Real.instNatCast (@DFunLike.coe (@ArithmeticFunction Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass)) Nat (fun x => Nat) (@ArithmeticFunction.instFunLikeNat Nat (@MulZeroClass.toZero Nat Nat.instMulZeroClass)) (ArithmeticFunction.sigma (@OfNat.ofNat Nat (nat_lit 1) (instOfNatNat (nat_lit 1)))) n)) (@HAdd.hAdd Real Real Real (@instHAdd Real Real.instAdd) (@Rat.cast Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)) (@HMul.hMul Real Real Real (@instHMul Real Real.instMul) (Real.exp (@Rat.cast Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n))) (Real.log (@Rat.cast Real Real.instRatCast (harmonic n)))))

It names 27 constants directly: Nat, Real, the order and arithmetic instances on them, the casts from Nat and Rat to Real, ArithmeticFunction.sigma, harmonic, Real.exp and Real.log. Its meaning depends on 1,801 Mathlib and core declarations in all, counting definitions with their bodies and theorems by their statements only (a proof cannot change what a definition means). The corresponding count for Robin's inequality is 2,050; the difference is mostly the definition of Euler's constant.

Files: the script, its output (both statements), and the dependency lists for Lagarias and Robin.

Downloads

The exported proof: output of lean4export on module Main. Unpacks to 61,570,595,788 bytes.

The exported challenge: the five statements with sorry proofs, importing only Mathlib. Unpacks to 350,862,970 bytes.

Smaller files:

comparator.json: Comparator config naming the checkers that can process this proof SHA256SUMS: hashes of everything on this page audit.log and Audit.lean: the axiom audit and the file that produced it project-oleans.sha256: sha256 of each of the 175,187 compiled files (29 MB). These hashes depend on the build directory; see the note below. nanoda.log: timing and exit status of the nanoda run sandbox-timeline.txt, sandbox-build.sh, sandbox-build-continue.sh and sandbox-project-oleans.sha256: the sandboxed lake build, its scripts and its per-file hashes (29 MB) con-leche-master.log and con-leche-compare.log: the two con-leche runs Check it yourself

With Lean v4.36.0 installed, nothing needs to be built. You need roughly 100 GB of RAM and 70 GB of disk.

zstd -d --long=30 solution.ndjson.zst # --long=30 is required zstd -d --long=27 challenge.ndjson.zst sha256sum solution.ndjson challenge.ndjson # compare with the hashes above lake comparator --config comparator.json \ --challenge-from-export challenge.ndjson --solution-from-export solution.ndjson

nanoda alone took about 28 minutes on 80 threads. The Lean kernels are single-threaded and take much longer.

The fastest independent check is con-leche built from source (Lean v4.36.0, about two minutes to build). It needs about 50 GB of RAM and took under four minutes on 64 threads:

Caveats How the original build was done, and the rebuild that checks it. The original build ran on cloud machines without a sandbox, and compiled each file by calling lean directly with the same inputs lake supplies (module name, package name and the lakefile's options), not through lake build. All the kernel checks above were run on the export from that build. We then repeated the build on a separate machine with lake build Main inside a bubblewrap sandbox: no network, the source tree read-only, only .lake writable, the archive downloaded afresh from the author's site, and Mathlib's files checked against the official cache first. The export made inside that sandbox is byte-identical to the published one, so every check on the published export applies to it. The per-file .olean hashes depend on the build directory, and one module is not deterministic. In Lean v4.33.1 a compiled file stores each linter message together with the absolute path of its source file. Of our 175,187 compiled files, 98,219 contain the path /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean/src/…; the other 76,968, including Main.olean, contain no path. So project-oleans.sha256 can be reproduced only by a build whose source tree is at /home/ubuntu/grh/src/lean; elsewhere, only the files of modules that emit no linter messages should match.The sandboxedlake build was run at that same path, and 175,186 of its 175,187 files are byte-identical to our manifest. Recompiling that one module six times on one machine with identical inputs gave one output four times and the other twice, and those are exactly the two hashes in the two manifests. The two outputs differ in 38 bytes: the name of one bound variable in BBtop.eq_1, an equation lemma that Lean generates automatically the first time a proof asks for it. Two adjacent theorems in the file both ask for it, Lean elaborates theorem bodies in parallel, and the lemma takes that variable's name from whichever theorem gets there first. Bound-variable names play no part in kernel checking, so the two files are logically the same. The export is not affected, and the export from the sandboxed build is byte-identical to ours: an export contains only the declarations that the five theorems depend on, and BBtop.eq_1 is not one of them, because the proofs that caused it to be generated do not refer to it. We checked that this name does not occur in the export. Had a proof on the dependency path referred to such a lemma by name, two builds could have produced exports with different hashes, although every check would still have passed on either. Compiled single-threaded (lean -j1), the module gave the same output six times out of six. A ten-line file with no imports reproduces the behaviour: on Lean v4.33.1 and v4.34.1 it compiles to two different outputs with -j32 and to one with -j1; on v4.36.0 it gave one output in 40 runs. The same race, with the first caller's options in place of its names, was reported as Lean issue #15498 and fixed by pull request #15499, first released in v4.36.0. That change also removes this behaviour: the file gives two outputs on the nightly builds of 7 and 8 October 2026 and one output in 40 runs on those of 9 and 10 October and on the toolchain built from the pull request alone. Because of this module, the sha256 of the whole manifest file is not reproducible even at the same path; compare file by file. A passing check shows that the formal statements, as written in Lean against Mathlib's definitions, follow from the three standard axioms according to the kernels used. It relies on those kernels and on Mathlib's definitions being what they are intended to be.

entry.title: PostgreSQL Extensions in Go
entry.content:
PostgreSQL extensions in Go

gopgext builds PostgreSQL extensions from plain Go code, using TinyGo. Mark a function with //gopgext:function and it becomes a SQL function: gopgext writes the C glue, the install script and the control file.

Just Go

A project is plain Go files. The standard library works: fmt, regexp, encoding/json, crypto/*, maps, generics, iterators, defer/recover.

Types map to SQL

Strings, numbers, arrays, NULLs, sets, rows, timestamps, UUIDs and JSON map to SQL types. Define your own data types and composite types in Go.

Queries and errors

Run SQL through SPI, return errors with SQLSTATE codes, log, read settings and stay responsive to query cancellation.

Beyond functions

Write triggers, aggregates, GiST, GIN, SP-GiST and BRIN operator classes, index access methods, foreign data wrappers and query hooks.

Proven on contrib

Ports of PostgreSQL’s contrib modules (pgcrypto, hstore, pg_stat_statements, cube, …) pass upstream’s regression tests.

Safe coexistence

Several Go extensions load in one backend. PostgreSQL errors never unwind through Go frames, and results are copied into PostgreSQL memory.

Hello, world# package main import ( "strings" "gopgext/pg" ) // Hello returns a greeting for name. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Hello(name string) string { return "Hello, " + name + "!" } // Shout upper-cases s. An empty string raises an error. // //gopgext:function immutable parallel=safe func Shout(s string) (string, error) { if s == "" { return "", pg.Errorf(pg.CodeInvalidParameterValue, "nothing to shout") } return strings.ToUpper(s) + "!", nil } func main() {} // runs once per backend, when PostgreSQL loads the library gopgext init hello # creates hello/go.mod and hello/main.go gopgext install hello # builds hello.so, hello.control, hello--1.0.sql and installs them psql -c 'CREATE EXTENSION hello' -c "SELECT hello('world')" # hello # --------------- # Hello, world!

The tutorial walks through it step by step.

A sibling project#

gopgext uses the same approach as gokm, which builds Linux kernel modules from Go: a custom TinyGo target and runtime layer for the host, a C runtime compiled by the host’s own build system (PGXS here, kbuild there), and generated glue.

entry.title: Inkling-2-Mini in 5.4 GB Memory
entry.content:
LookAtMyQuant is a quantization compiler. It measures how much each stored piece of a model hurts the output when compressed. It then picks a code for each piece so the whole model fits a size budget with the least damage.

On Gemma 4 E2B, its GGUF has 12× lower KL than Q4_K_M at the same file size. The method and every result are on the site.

The code is under the MIT license.

LookAtMyQuant 2 takes Qwen3.5-4B to 1.23 GB, 2.3 bits per weight. The file solves 330 of 540 exact-answer math problems. Prism ML's Bonsai 2 Ternary 4B solves 328 at 1.20 GB, and the original solves 359. Its KL from the original on held-out text is 0.45 nats, against 0.59 for Bonsai.

The recipe is post-training quantization with trellis codes, calibrated on the model's own worked math solutions with digit tokens weighted 10×, and with bits allocated per row by Fisher information. 4,000 steps of distillation follow, in which every layer is re-quantized once from the original weights. The page has the findings, the full recipe and its cost, about $34 of GPU time.

The recipe's code is here, and the next section runs it. The 1.23 GB file itself is the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release, packed for the Apple Silicon runtime.

The same recipe takes Qwen3.8-27B from 53.7 GB to 7.2 GB, 2.1 bits per weight, calibrated and distilled on English prose and chat, code and math. The file solves 401 of the 540 math problems, as many as the original, and Unsloth's UD-IQ2_XXS GGUF of the same size solves 348. It also scores above that GGUF on HumanEval (73.8% against 67.1%), MMLU (78.8% against 75.0%) and GSM8K (94.5% against 92.7%).

Beside it sits a 4-bit DSpine drafter (1.02 GB, converted from tencent/Qwen3.8-27B-DSpine-b16 with runtime_mlx/convert_dspine.py and packed with pack_drafter.py), which roughly doubles decode speed on math and code on Apple silicon.

Extended to a 26.4B physical / 5.4B active 3×-looped MoE (L6–17 looped 3× = 48 logical visits, 128 experts top-8), the compiler and full-MoE proximal fine-tuning (SQYFR / SQYFR v2) compress thinkingmachines/Inkling-2-Mini from 18.89 GB of text weights into six Apple Silicon MLX builds spanning 8 GB iPhones up to lossless teacher parity: 3.85 GB (1.18 bpp), 4.72 GB (1.45 bpp), 5.38 GB (1.65 bpp), 8.87 GB (2.72 bpp), 11.18 GB (3.43 bpp), and 12.76 GB (3.92 bpp) — combining 4 KB SRAM hashed block-vector trellis codes (ht2/ht3), row trellis codes (rtr1/rtr4), dedicated attention projection floors, a tr2 floor on the tail lm_head bucket (head.7), and exact native NVFP4 passthrough (69/192 and 109/192 highest-sensitivity expert buckets kept at 0.0 error in the 11.2 GB and 12.8 GB builds).

Evaluated untruncated (max_new_tokens = 1,536, greedy, reasoning_effort="none") on the same BF16 teacher, openai/gsm8k (test[:200]), all 164 executable openai/openai_humaneval problems (strict <|content_text|> execution across every build), 4 Vision VQA tests (with the untouched 637 MB BF16 vision tower), and 16+13-language TextMix windows:

Model Text GB Text bpp free_KL (en/chat/code) all13_KL GSM8K (200) HumanEval Strict (164) Vision (4) 3-Task Mean vs Teacher Original BF16 Teacher 18.89 5.80 0.0000 0.0000 193 / 200 (96.5%) 152 / 164 (92.7%) 4 / 4 100.0% LookAtMyQuant 12.8 GB (NVFP4 + Trellis) 12.76 3.92 0.0070 0.0268 193 / 200 (96.5%) 152 / 164 (92.7%) 4 / 4 100.0% LookAtMyQuant 11.2 GB (NVFP4 + Trellis) 11.18 3.43 0.0115 0.0400 190 / 200 (95.0%) 151 / 164 (92.1%) 4 / 4 99.3% (98.9% pooled) LookAtMyQuant 8.9 GB (SQYFR) 8.87 2.72 0.0208 0.0571 192 / 200 (96.0%) 149 / 164 (90.9%) 4 / 4 99.2% (98.9% pooled) LookAtMyQuant 5.4 GB (SQYFR v2) 5.38 1.65 0.0864 0.2773 174 / 200 (87.0%) 117 / 164 (71.3%) 4 / 4 89.0% (84.5% pooled) LookAtMyQuant 4.7 GB (SQYFR v2, 12 GB iPhone) 4.72 1.45 0.1196 0.3988 165 / 200 (82.5%) 110 / 164 (67.1%) 4 / 4 86.0% (79.9% pooled) LookAtMyQuant 3.9 GB (SQYFR v2, 8 GB iPhone) 3.85 1.18 0.2215 0.6335 157 / 200 (78.5%) 79 / 164 (48.2%) 4 / 4 77.8% (68.8% pooled)

At 12.76 GB, Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-12.8GB matches 100.0% of the untouched BF16 teacher on every benchmark (349 / 349 pooled) in 32.5% less text weight memory. Both 11.18 GB and 8.87 GB retain 99.2–99.3% 3-task mean (345 / 349 = 98.9% pooled), with 8.87 GB cutting KL 2.34× on English/chat/code (0.0208 vs 0.0486) and 29.6% across all 13 languages (0.0571 vs 0.0811) below Unsloth's 9.14 GB UD-Q2_K_XL GGUF. Below 2 bpp, SQYFR v2 (jointly training all 24.46B MoE experts and 130–144 attention trellis projections on position-0-aligned BF16 teacher <|content_thinking|> -> <|content_text|> rollouts with 6.0× control-boundary weighting, full-rank live Hessian projections, and 250 exact-P continuous scale + steering polish steps) lifts 5.38 GB (1.65 bpp) to 90.0% top-1 agreement (free_KL = 0.0864), 87.0% GSM8K, and 71.3% strict HumanEval (117 / 164), lifts 4.72 GB (1.45 bpp, sized to fit under the 12 GB iPhone 5.99 GiB Jetsam ceiling alongside the 179 MB drafter at 4.35 GiB active / 5.35 GiB decode peak) to 82.5% GSM8K and 67.1% strict HumanEval (110 / 164), and rescues 3.85 GB (1.18 bpp, 3.54 GiB active / 4.57 GiB decode peak for 8 GB devices) from static PTQ collapse (1.0% GSM8K, 1.8% HumanEval) to 78.5% GSM8K (157 / 200), 48.2% strict HumanEval (79 / 164), and 4 / 4 Vision.

All six run through lamq and runtime_mlx via unified single-launch Metal kernels (UnifiedMoESide mixing unrotated NVFP4 and Hadamard-rotated trellis experts across decode, speculative verify, and M5 MetalPerformancePrimitives prefill + FlashAttention-2 SDPA + exact unbiased temp > 0 speculative sampling), optionally paired with the 178.9 MB 4-bit DSpark drafters: on Apple M5 Max, 12.8 GB reaches 2,016 tok/s T=512 prefill, 60.5 tok/s serial, and 112.7 tok/s median lossless drafted decode (119.2 tok/s math, 106.2 tok/s code; 12.72 GB active RAM); 11.2 GB reaches 2,032 tok/s prefill, 62.4 tok/s serial, and 103.7 tok/s median (111.7 tok/s math; 11.13 GB active RAM); 8.9 GB decodes at 63.5 tok/s serial and 106.0 tok/s median (125.8 tok/s reasoning, 123.8 tok/s math; 9.41 GB active RAM); 5.4 GB reaches 1,807 tok/s prefill, 75.3 tok/s serial, and 124.4 tok/s median (142.9 tok/s math, 126.5 tok/s reasoning; 5.33 GB active RAM); 4.7 GB decodes up to 122.6 tok/s on math (98.7 tok/s median, 3.53 tok/check; 4.68 GB active RAM); and 3.9 GB decodes at 75.5 tok/s serial and 103.1 tok/s median (117.9 tok/s math, 128.3 tok/s short math; 3.81 GB active RAM).

On Apple silicon, install the runtime package directly (this installs mlx, mlx-lm, numpy, and huggingface-hub without the PyTorch compiler dependencies):

pip install git+https://github.com/ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant.git

From a local clone, pip install -e . installs the lamq command, or run python -m runtime_mlx without installing.

Command line. Pass either a local model folder or a Hugging Face repo ID:

lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \ -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \ --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter \ -p "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals." --stats lamq chat shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB \ --drafter shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-12.8GB \ --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \ -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-5.4GB \ --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \ -p "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps." --stats lamq generate shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-4.7GB \ --drafter shinmegamiboson/Inkling-2-Mini-LookAtMyQuant-drafter \ -p "Write a Python function that merges overlapping intervals." --stats

lamq generate reads stdin when -p is omitted, supports --raw, --system, --thinking, --temp, --mode linear|chat-fork|copy-wide, --no-adaptive, and --json. lamq info <model> inspects a packed model's format and dimensions without loading weights.

Python integration. runtime_mlx.load returns an (model, tokenizer) pair compatible with mlx_lm.generate and mlx_lm.stream_generate (auto-detecting opgraph-packed-1 models such as Qwen3.5-4B / Qwen3.8-27B, inkling2-packed models such as Inkling-2-Mini, and lamq.json exports such as Gemma 4 E2B):

from mlx_lm import generate from runtime_mlx import load model, tok = load("shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB") prompt = tok.apply_chat_template( [{"role": "user", "content": "What is 17 times 23? Show the steps."}], add_generation_prompt=True, enable_thinking=False, ) print(generate(model, tok, prompt, max_tokens=200))

For streaming, multi-turn chat, or speculative decoding through one interface, use Runtime:

from runtime_mlx import Runtime rt = Runtime.load( "shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB", drafter="shinmegamiboson/Qwen3.8-27B-LookAtMyQuant-7.2GB-drafter", ) for chunk in rt.stream("Solve 3x + 4y = 31 and 5x - 2y = 17.", max_tokens=256): print(chunk.text, end="", flush=True)

Install the dependencies and download the model and WikiText-2. The code reads SmolLM2-360M's config when it starts, so do this first.

pip install -r requirements.txt python -c "from huggingface_hub import snapshot_download as d; d('HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M')" python -c "from datasets import load_dataset as l; l('Salesforce/wikitext', 'wikitext-2-raw-v1')"

Measure. This compresses one piece at a time, leaves the rest exact, and records the KL to the original model. The full set for this model, 2,312 measurements, took about 50 minutes on an L40S.

python compiler.py measure --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --part linear --layers 0-3 --out results/batch/my_measurements.json

Allocate. This picks one code per piece, with the least summed KL inside the budget. It needs no GPU. This command uses the SmolLM2-360M measurements in this repository, with a budget of 3.044 bits per weight.

python compiler.py allocate --sens 'results/batch/ccSens*.json' --target disk --items linear --bits 3.044 --out results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json

The plan it writes has the same widths as results/compiler/plans/sm_lin_3044.json.

Build and score. This quantizes the model to the plan, one matrix at a time. It then reports perplexity and KL to the original on WikiText-2 test.

python quantize.py --program plan --model HuggingFaceTB/SmolLM2-360M --plan results/compiler/plans/my_plan.json --out results/my_run.json

Our run of that plan is in results/batch/cc_sm_lin_3044.json. It reached perplexity 16.64 and KL 0.0926, against an original perplexity of 15.31. Add --layers 1 --calib 8 --eval 2 for a quick check that everything works.

Each step is a named job; python run_batch.py --list prints its command. The jobs need Qwen3.5-4B in models/Qwen3.5-4B on the volume and the text mix (modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text). Every file they make goes to lm2/ on the volume.

modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Text modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Calibration,lm2Solutions modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2RowImportance modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Build modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Finetune modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs lm2Math,lm2Math216,lm2TextKL Job Script What it does Our run lm2Text other_text.py The original answers science, code, instruction and tool prompts, and MATH and GSM8K training problems. This also downloads MATH lm2Calibration math_calibration.py The calibration set: the original's greedy solutions to 384 MATH training problems, in 2,048-token windows 15 minutes, H100 lm2Solutions checked_solutions.py The math text the fine-tuning distils on: solutions to MATH problems and to math_bench.py problems from another seed, with wrong calculations corrected and only right answers kept 33 minutes, H100 lm2RowImportance row_importance.py Each output row's Fisher information at digit-predicting positions 1 minute, H100 lm2Build quantize.py Post-training quantization: trellis codes along rows, digit tokens weighted 10× in the Hessians, QEP at α = 0.5, bits per row from the row plan, e-means codebooks 37 minutes, H100 lm2Finetune finetune.py 4,000 steps of distillation on latent weights pulled toward their codes, with every layer re-quantized once from the original weights 2.7 hours, B200 lm2Math, lm2Math216 math_eval.py The 540-problem benchmark and a second set of 216, for the original, Bonsai, the build and the fine-tuned build 20 minutes a model, H100 lm2TextKL text_kl.py KL from the original on WikiText-2 and on the text mix's 13 sources 1 minute a model, H100

lm2BuildSmoke, lm2FinetuneSmoke and lm2MathSmoke run the same code on two layers, 60 steps and 36 problems, in a few minutes each.

The row plan. lm2Build reads results/compiler/rows/q35_rowplan_1p2GB.json, which gives 1 to 4 bits to each of 1,520 row groups. row_allocation.py made it. Its build-control command builds and packs a control with a fixed split of rows, prepare-rows allocates rows inside the control's packed bytes with rowgroup_alloc.py, and build-rows builds under the plan and checks the packed size against it.

The codebooks. The four e-means codebooks the build decodes with are in cache/codes/. --trellis-fit lloyd gives the earlier ones, and a plan made before the change keeps them unless the flag says otherwise.

Recent equal-byte recipe improvements. Two zero-byte additions are available in the compiler and fine-tuning scripts:

Softmax-Fisher token table ranking (--embed-order sfisher-mix in compiler.py measure and quantize.py). Ranks tied embedding/output buckets by a 50/50 blend of output Softmax-Fisher E[p_v (1 - p_v)] and corpus frequency (and untied output heads by Softmax-Fisher alone). Mid-training equal-byte row reallocation (--realloc-at 1000 in finetune.py). Paired with --rebuild-at 1000, measures each layer's continuous-vs-stored proximal KL gap KL(all P) - KL(layer = W) to shift bits toward deep unabsorbed layers while keeping exact file size (--realloc-max-delta 1). Combined with sfisher-mix on Qwen3.5-4B at identical 1.23 GB (2.297 bpp), WikiText-2 KL fell from 0.425 to 0.387 (−9.0%) and 13-source KL from 0.447 to 0.378 (−15.5%, improving all 13 sources).

Where these jobs differ from our run. Our GSM8K solutions were written earlier, with thinking always off. Our text KL on 13 sources used 52 windows picked from the text mix by a separate tool; --sources mix takes the mix's own evaluation windows, on which our file scores 0.44 where the page reports 0.45.

run_batch.py names every job, and modal_app.py runs them. modal_fetch.py downloads models and the text mix used for calibration and evaluation.

modal run modal_app.py::setup modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --text modal run --detach modal_fetch.py --models google/gemma-4-E2B-it modal run --detach modal_app.py --jobs ccMG4E2Noise,ccMG4E2Spot,ccMG4E2EmbKv

The runs behind the site used these machines, each with 8 CPU cores:

Model GPU Time SmolLM2-360M L40S About 50 minutes to measure, in 9 parallel jobs Gemma 4 E2B, measuring H100 7–26 minutes per job, in 4 jobs Gemma 4 E2B, building a plan H100 28–58 minutes per plan

gguf_compiler.py makes plans out of llama.cpp's own tensor types, so the result runs in llama.cpp as it is. public_eval.py scores public quantizations the same way as our plans. Both run inside the image in modal_gguf.py, which builds llama.cpp with CUDA.

quantize.py --export <folder> writes a plan in the format runtime_mlx/ reads. A plan with trellis codes also needs --trellis-rows 16,8, which runs each trellis path along a row of its matrix, so that decoding an entry reads only that row. On Apple silicon, pip install . installs mlx and mlx-lm; requirements.txt holds the PyTorch compiler dependencies.

On Gemma 4 E2B at 2.5 GB, the trellis plan has 26% lower KL than the Lloyd–Max plan and decodes about 22% slower. runtime_mlx/test_trellis_gen.py and runtime_mlx/test_trellis.py check the trellis kernels against the matrices the quantizer built.

python runtime_mlx/bench.py lamq path/to/export

runtime_mlx/fast_q35.py decodes the packed 1.2 GB Qwen3.5-4B file one token at a time, straight from its trellis codes. runtime_mlx/drafter_q35.py adds speculative decoding. A small drafter proposes the seven tokens after the model's latest one in a single pass. The model then checks all eight positions in one pass over its coded weights (runtime_mlx/block_q35.py) and keeps the proposals that match its own choice, so the text is exactly its own greedy text.

On an M5 Max, over 30 held-out prompts of up to 256 tokens, generation with the drafter was 2.0 times as fast: 176 tokens a second against 88, timed in alternation in one process on 2026-11-11. A check kept 4.3 tokens on average. Over eight everyday prompts it was 1.5 times as fast. The gain follows how predictable the text is: 2.5 times on algebra, 2.0 on code, 1.2 on chat and 1.05 on a story, and one of the 30 held-out prompts ran slower with the drafter. The text matched plain greedy decoding on every prompt. These are speeds after the first token; reading the prompt takes about 0.1 s either way.

Two later changes are in this code. Each was measured against the version before it on 40 paired generations: proposing from the 96,033 most common tokens was 6.0% faster, and picking the winning token inside the packed product was 5.3% faster. Linear mode also enables self-calibrating adaptive fallback by default (adaptive=True; pass --no-adaptive to disable): when rolling acceptance drops below the measured break-even ratio of drafted-check latency to serial-step latency (accounting for cache flush and drafter context replay), it pauses drafting for short exact serial bursts and resumes once acceptance recovers, preserving bit-exact greedy parity while avoiding slowdowns on low-acceptance prose.

The drafter is a DSpine model, trained with SpecForge from the published DFlash drafter for Qwen3.5-4B on the 1.2 GB file's own greedy answers. modal_drafter.py runs the training as one Modal job, and it cost $42. On 300 held-out prompts the trained drafter gets 4.65 tokens per check, against 4.30 for the stock DFlash drafter.

pack_drafter.py stores the drafter at 4 bits a weight in the build's own code, with no calibration data: 464 MB against 1.83 GB at 16 bits. On 60 held-out prompts the 4-bit drafter kept 4.35 tokens per check against 4.38, and the text was the same. drafter_q35.py loads either form and writes the packed one out dense as it loads. The 4-bit drafter is the lm2-drafter-4bit release. It runs beside the packed 1.2 GB file, the lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb release.

gh release download lm2-qwen35-4b-1.2gb --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D q35-1.2gb gh release download lm2-drafter-4bit --repo ShinMegamiBoson/lookatmyquant -D drafter-4bit python runtime_mlx/bench_drafted.py q35-1.2gb drafter-4bit

A use-after-free in Ghostscript’s Type 1 font loader lets a crafted document cross Ghostscript’s -dSAFER sandbox, alter native path controls, and execute attacker-chosen commands as the rendering process.

Ghostscript sits beneath print, email, upload, and preview workflows. Our ImageMagick research showed how files named .png or .jpg can still reach Ghostscript through image conversion. The index below records confirmed affected paths alongside additional applications whose renderer routes we traced.

Upload2Shell / public record

From the first escape to the downstream reports, fixes, and publication.

We found a Type 1 font-loader path out of Ghostscript's -dSAFER boundary. A crafted document gained native access inside the rendering process.

A signed-out request for an attacker-hosted file reached Ghostscript in Google's document renderer. We sent the production proof to Google.

Core's upload path exposed the renderer to Author+ users and any Contributor granted upload_files. Public upload fields in multiple plugins required no WordPress login. WordPress shipped its separate CVE-2026-65640 fix.

We filed the Type 1 loader flaw upstream as Artifex Bug 709684. Our broader audit also produced other independent Ghostscript findings.

Artifex released the fix for the Type 1 loader flaw.

We confirmed a production document-processing finding in our broader Ghostscript research. Its individual root and proof belong to a separate case study.

Ghostscript 10.08.0 entered Debian unstable. The Debian 13 security update followed later.

Confirmed unauthenticated remote command execution: an IPP job to a shared queue ran on the host as lp. We sent the network reproduction to Debian Security.

Confirmed remote execution after an external sender's attachment was thumbnailed when its email was viewed. The tested ImageMagick delegate ran the proof as www-data.

Confirmed command execution in the Roundcube thumbnail path shipped with Plesk Obsidian. We reported the result to WebPros.

Confirmed unauthenticated remote command execution through a public registration widget with an upload field enabled. We reported the route to the plugin team.

Confirmed unauthenticated remote command execution through a public PDF form configured to store files in the WordPress Media Library. We sent the report to the plugin team.

Confirmed a production route in our broader Ghostscript research. The individual access path, root, and proof will appear with its case study.

entry.title: Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs
entry.content:
Advice for the next 100 Rust GUIs Raph Levien, November 21, 2026

This is a followup to Advice for the next dozen Rust GUIs, published 4.5 years ago. The world is different in many ways, but some of the advice there is still valid. There have been roughly 20 Rust GUI toolkits announced since that blog post (see 2026 survey), but also a recent rapid acceleration of interest in Rust GUI, fueled by AI.

Rust GUI is still compelling

The motivation to build GUI apps in Rust remains strong. Many shipping GUI apps suffer from poor performance, especially when built with cross-platform technology. GUI toolkits shipped by platforms have largely stagnated, and system vendors remain uninterested in solving the cross-platform problem, so Electron has grown in popularity. RAM remains expensive and the focus is shifting to mobile, so bloat has real consequences. Building high-performance UI in Rust is a practical alternative.

Adoption of Rust UI in the past few years has been slow. Few flagship apps use Rust for their UI. One of the most notable is the Zed editor, built on their own GPUI framework. It proves that shipping Rust UI is practical, and indeed, GPUI is emerging as a major choice for AI-driven rewrites, most notably Discord. My personal sense is that GPUI is well suited to the Zed use case, and shipping in a real project boosts its visibility and credibility quite a bit, but it’s not necessarily the ideal choice for more general purpose applications. Among other things, its 2D rendering engine is well suited to a text editor, but lacks full gradient support, blending, filters, and other features expected of a renderer in the same class as Vello or Skia.

The reasons for slow adoption may be melting away. Writing Rust code is harder than languages more traditionally used for UI (TypeScript, Kotlin, Swift), and finding engineers skilled in both Rust and UI is challenging. But AI is changing the game. There’s evidence that the LLM cost of writing Rust code is not significantly higher than other languages, and there is reason to believe that in large codebases, Rust will be more maintainable because its type system helps enforce invariants. So if all languages have roughly the same cost, then why not go with one that has a dramatically better combination of safety and performance?

For these reasons, Rust is rapidly becoming the language for AI rewrites of existing codebases. But there is still no consensus on the strategy for the UI layer. I predict there will be a small explosion of trying lots of different things.

Native is complicated

My 2022 blog post had a large section on “native,” first pointing out that the term has no clear meaning, and more broadly pointing out that “native” UI toolkits are simply choices among many, and should be evaluated on the important quality criteria.

I think this is largely still true, but it depends greatly on which platform is being targeted. Windows still has no clear native choice (see Microsoft Hasn’t Had a Coherent GUI Strategy Since Petzold) and on Mac there is a bit of fragmentation between AppKit and SwiftUI. However, SwiftUI has performance issues (see Michael Tsai blog from 2025) and so it is clearly possible to do better on the performance front.

While desktop UI has remained stagnant, the situation on mobile is a bit different. Platforms continue to invest, and there are many fine details that are important for an app to look and feel native. One very notable example is Liquid Glass on iOS – if you use UIKit or SwiftUI, you can get that with little effort, but apps built with cross-platform toolkits won’t quite seem right. In addition, making gesture recognition, scroll dynamics, and IME 100% match the platform are not yet fully solved problems.

Thus, for mobile, an extremely viable path is to use the native toolkit for UI but do the common “business logic” in Rust. I’m not sure about the business logic, but for the UI, this is the decision that Shopify has made recently, abandoning React Native. I believe 1Password has this architecture. This is also the "Phoenix" plan for Discord on mobile, while using GPUI on desktop.

That said, there's been considerable progress in trying to build mobile UI entirely in Rust. Below is a short screencast of the editor demo in android-view. You can see that a lot of IME functionality works, including swiping, moving the cursor by rolling the space bar, and deleting in semantic chunks. Not shown in the video below, but composition regions (needed for CJK) also work, and there's basic accessibility through AccessKit.

Text layout and accessibility infrastructure is basically solved

One of the big unsolved problems as of the 2022 blog post was text layout. It is of course a hard problem to get right. I’m pleased to say that the ecosystem now has a good solution, in the form of Parley. It’s gotten there as a result of sustained investment from Google, Canva, and Dioxus (now Cognition), as well as contributions from the community. It seems to be used in the majority of new Rust UI toolkits. In addition, to help mitigate the risk of monoculture, Cosmic Text is a viable alternative.

AccessKit was just getting started in 2022, but is now solid infrastructure as well, and used by most UI toolkits. I should note, though, there is a difference between a good integration and a box ticking exercise. And there is more work to be done, for example to make rich text editing fully accessible. One other problem I'd like to see addressed is performance degradation when accessibility is enabled. This is a problem for egui in particular, as it has to build and diff a tree each animation frame, undercutting the benefits of its underlying immediate mode design.

System compositor is still unsolved

One topic I talked about extensively in the 2022 blog post is leveraging the system compositor. This issue is even more pressing today, especially with the increased importance of video. You really want a video playing in a hardware accelerated layer when possible, and on low end devices it’s the only hope for getting smooth frame rates.

There has been some progress, notably the subduction library, but it certainly isn’t commonly integrated into UI toolkits yet. To do it well is a challenging problem, as the capabilities provided by the platform vary widely. Ideally there’s a rich and high level interface, something like CALayer on Apple platforms, and polyfills to implement that interface as well as possible on other platforms. On Android, when the task is something simple, like overlaying some GUI controls on a video, it would use SurfaceFlinger layers, but when it involves more sophisticated compositing, it would run shaders on the GPU.

This is absolutely something we should build, ideally as a high quality community project rather than something with dozens of vibe-coded forks. But even in the latter case it’s better for it to exist than not.

Immediate vs retained mode

One of the challenges of the Rust UI ecosystem is that different applications have different needs. The idea of a single, unified UI for completely general purpose use may be behind us, especially now that LLMs can optimize and fine tune for specific use cases.

That’s been playing out architecturally in the choice between immediate mode and retained mode. Immediate mode is very appealing because it’s less total code and seems quite a bit simpler. And for some applications (most especially development support for games) it works well. However, I am concerned it won’t scale especially well. In short, it’s good at the first 90%, but it makes the second 90% harder. To be considered really production-ready, it has to establish stable widget identities to build and update the accessibility tree, and it has to reliably cache expensive intermediate artifacts such as text layouts (simple immediate mode often gets around this by cutting corners in text layout, which may be fine for gamedev). And of course, it pulls strongly towards a model of re-rendering everything every frame rather than exploiting layers in the compositor.

For this reason among others, I am not impressed by the choice of the ArtCraft projects to use egui. I do think egui is a really good implementation of the immediate mode paradigm in Rust, and it does solve a number of problems (including accessibility, something mainline Iced does not yet support), but it wouldn’t be my first choice for productivity and design applications. The egui README is quite honest on the advantages and disadvantages, and is worth consulting.

Clearly defined modules

One theme that’s emerging from trying to do LLM-assisted software engineering well is having clearly scoped modules, ideally with solid specifications of what the module does. Within a module, given clear objectives such as performance and robustness against adverse inputs, an LLM can do very well.

This philosophy is in tension with what has historically worked well. People reasonably choose a UI toolkit based on how good it looks. In particular, Apple UI frameworks have an immense amount of design knowledge baked in, especially in the defaults. With very little effort, it’s possible for a developer to make an app that looks and feels like a Mac app, even if not very polished.

I think in the future we should be moving toward a separation of design and execution. Both are hard problems, but very different. I’m especially excited about how much room there is to improve the execution side when really optimizing. As discussed in the 2022 blog post, the computer science core of a UI toolkit is an incremental computation engine.

Having a good spec at the interface between design and execution is critically important. As a general strategy, I suggest adapting web standards, but not following them slavishly. Web standards are an impressive and important artifact. A huge amount of time and energy has gone into producing them, and there’s also a lot of care to making things work cross-platform. The extensive WPT tests are the true magic of the spec, aiding correctness in the multiple high quality open source implementations. All this goes a long way to explaining why Electron is popular.

That said, strictly adhering to web standards has serious downsides. DOM is slow and memory-intensive; a lighter weight tree representation with a bulk mutation interface might serve the need of GUI apps better. Full CSS style resolution and layout is also expensive, though CSS is a rich and powerful way to describe styling. A subset of CSS carefully curated for efficiency might be useful. I’ve done experiments in implementing selectors as an efficient state machine that supports incremental evaluation, at the expense of fancier CSS features such as sibling selectors.

The Web is also lacking a solid way to represent virtualized lists, a core feature of every efficient UI toolkit. A spec here requires nailing down the interface with the data model, preserving incrementality.

Blitz, as a modular browser engine, is well placed to serve as the cornerstone of hybrid approaches borrowing heavily from Web specs, but also adapting them to be higher performance and more tightly integrated with platform capabilities. As just one example, it’s possible to start with Stylo as the CSS selector engine, and then replace it with a leaner, more efficient CSS engine if that proves to be practical.

One good example of separation of concerns into smaller modules is the Xilem/Masonry split. The Xilem reactive layer was designed to be independent of the actual elements it controls, and indeed it has instantiations both for DOM (which, among other things, is the infrastructure for the squircle interactive demo) and Masonry widgets. Masonry, on the other hand, was designed to be independent of the reactive layer and indeed the language for the layer above it.

By contrast, SwiftUI mashes together the low level widget implementation, the reactivity framework, and the language as well; Swift runtime reflection is part of the execution engine. Obviously SwiftUI has had a lot farther reach than Xilem, but my argument today is that we should reconsider assumptions as things are rapidly changing.

Optimization opportunities

Given a UI design encoded in a certain way – which can be code, data, or a combination of the two in a DSL – an engine has a number of opportunities to optimize the execution of that design. Perhaps a lot of this section is gilding the lily, as a straightforward evaluation of the design in optimized Rust code will outperform almost any shipping GUI. But I’m interested in the limits of what performance is possible. Can we get silky smooth UI even on low end Android phones? I think the answer is yes, and the question worth exploring.

One useful tactic may be separating out the static from the dynamic parts of the design, and precomputing the static parts. That in no way precludes the design having dynamic parts; it's just that it may be possible to avoid the cost of a fully dynamic implementation.

Another fruitful avenue for optimization is optimizing the use of layers, to be composited either using the system compositor or a lightweight GPU-accelerated polyfill. Using layers effectively can dramatically improve performance, mostly by avoiding re-rendering of parts of the interface that haven't changed. However, layers have a RAM cost, and using too many layers can actually slow things down, as allocating new layers has to go through calls to the underlying system. Getting this right is a tricky optimization problem, and a good use of either measurement or analysis. UI toolkits generally either use heuristics, which are not always perfect, or explicit hints (like .drawingGroup() in SwiftUI or RepaintBoundary in Flutter).

For a deeper dive into performance questions, see A Critique of GPUI. Ideally, there aren't huge performance differences between UI toolkits, as all low hanging fruit should be picked. We expect implementations of system languages to be quite comparable in performance, but still tolerate wide discrepancies in GUI performance.

Advice Be bold. Now is the time. Rust UI has the potential to deliver vastly higher performance than the status quo. Build on solid foundations. Use well-defined specs when available. Find ways to work well with open source. Work with upstream but don’t spam them with slop PRs. Acknowledgements

Thanks to Nico Burns for reviewing an earlier draft of this post.

entry.title: PcapAnalyzer – self-hosted pcap analyzer with 27 problem detectors
entry.content:
Versión en español: README.es.md.

Find the network fault in seconds, not hours. Upload a .pcap / .pcapng capture (gzip too) and PcapAnalyzer tells you what is failing, why, and what to check next. It runs on your own machine, so captures never leave your network.

Free and open source (Apache 2.0). Status: beta.

Try it without installing anything: https://pcap-analyzer-seven.vercel.app/#demo Download: https://sebaandrada6.gumroad.com/l/hspgx (free) or clone this repository. 27 detectors that run on every capture, each with a severity and a next step: TCP: firewall blocks (SYN→RST), retransmissions, duplicate ACKs, loss and reordering, zero and full windows, resets after the handshake, slow handshakes.Path: PMTUD black holes, low MSS, IP fragmentation, ICMP errors, routing loops.Name and address services: unanswered or slow DNS, SERVFAIL, NXDOMAIN bursts, DHCP NAK / DECLINE / no answer, duplicate IPs, ARP storms.Applications: HTTP 4xx / 5xx and slow responses, TLS alerts, SSL 3.0 / TLS 1.0 / 1.1.Tunnels: IPsec (IKE and ESP), WireGuard, OpenVPN, GRE, L2TP and Teredo that are one-way, never answer a handshake or keep renegotiating.Security: port scans and sweeps, cleartext logins (FTP, POP3, IMAP, SMTP AUTH, HTTP Basic; credentials are never stored or shown), Telnet / SMBv1 / SNMP v1-v2c, ARP spoofing, overlapping IP fragments. Capture quality first. It warns when the capture itself limits the result: frames duplicated by a mirror port, traffic seen in one direction only, truncated packets, connections already open when the capture started. Wireshark-style views: packet list with real Wireshark display filters over the whole capture, colouring, CSV export, expert info, HTTP / DNS / DHCP / TLS tables, response times and a flow diagram per conversation. AI investigation (optional): an AI investigates the capture with tools (real filters, stream detail, statistics) and cites the packets behind every claim. You can then ask follow-up questions. It uses your own Anthropic API key; without one, a demo mode runs the full flow with text generated from the analysis, at no cost. PDF report, Spanish and English interface, light and dark theme.

You need Docker with Docker Compose. On Windows, run the script from Git Bash or WSL.

git clone https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer.git cd PcapAnalyzer ./start.sh

The script creates a random access token (shown once, stored in .env) and starts the app. When the build finishes, open http://localhost:8080, paste the token into the "API token" field (top right) and upload a capture, or click "Try the sample capture".

The app listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Do not expose it on a network without an authenticated reverse proxy: the API can use your AI account. QUICKSTART.md has the details, the AI setup and troubleshooting.

You need Python 3.9+, Node 20+ and tshark (installed with Wireshark).

cd backend python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/pip install -r requirements-dev.txt export API_TOKENS="$(openssl rand -hex 32)" .venv/bin/uvicorn app.main:app --reload cd frontend npm install npm run dev

Open http://localhost:5173 and paste the same token. If tshark is not on your PATH, set TSHARK_PATH to the binary.

The capture is analysed on your machine. While an AI investigation lasts it is kept encrypted (60 minutes of inactivity, or until you press "Delete capture now") and is then deleted. The AI is optional. It only sees what its tools return (packet metadata; packet content only if you switch it on for that session), never the pcap file. No telemetry and no accounts for the self-hosted version. cd backend && .venv/bin/python -m pytest -q # needs tshark cd frontend && npm test

PcapAnalyzer is a beta. It has been tested with synthetic fixtures and public sample captures, and the most useful feedback is a capture where it misses a problem or reports one that is not real. Please open an issue at https://github.com/sebaandrada-cell/PcapAnalyzer/issues and describe the case. Do not attach captures that contain real credentials or customer data; anonymise them first or describe the pattern.

The technical reference (JSON schema, detector thresholds, limits, API errors) is in README.es.md, in Spanish.

Apache License 2.0. See NOTICE for third-party software: tshark / Wireshark (GPL) runs as a separate program and is not distributed with PcapAnalyzer.
